When you go to renew a driver’s license you’ll be asked to demonstrate that your vision meets the local minimum standards (usually 20/40 or better).  

**What to bring**

| Item | Why it helps |
|------|--------------|
| **Your regular corrective lenses** (glasses or contacts) | The licensing office will ask you to read a chart — you’ll need the lenses you normally use to pass the test. |
| **A spare pair of glasses** (or an extra set of contacts) | If a lens is lost, broken, or you experience sudden dryness or irritation on the day, a backup lets you still meet the vision requirement without a repeat test. |
| **Recent eye‑exam documentation** (if you had a comprehensive exam within the past 12 months) | Some jurisdictions allow you to skip the on‑site vision screening if you can show a recent examiner’s report confirming adequate visual acuity. The summary of Session 37 notes that **annual comprehensive exams** are the standard checkpoint for any changes in vision. |
| **Any prescribed reading or bifocal lenses** (if you normally need them for near vision) | Even if the road‑test uses a distance chart, the office may ask you to demonstrate near vision for “reading the license” tasks. |

**Do you need any special “vision‑related backup” beyond this?**  

- No extra testing equipment is required; the DMV’s own chart is sufficient.  
- Bring only the correction you normally wear (plus a spare) unless you have a known **dry‑eye** or **fluctuating vision** condition (see Session 37). In that case, schedule a quick check‑up before the renewal to avoid an unexpected failure.  

**Bottom line:** Plan to bring your everyday glasses or contacts **and** a spare pair. If you have a recent comprehensive eye exam (the one recommended in the post‑surgical care checklist), bring that report as optional proof of good vision. No other vision‑related items are typically needed.
